'''Iranian Sign Language''' (ISL), also referred to as Farsi Sign Language, Persian Sign Language, and Zaban Eshareh Irani (ZEI, {{Langx|fa|زبان اشاره ایرانی}}), is the sign language used by [[Deafness|Deaf]] and [[hard-of-hearing]] people in [[Iran]]. It is a true sign language, unlike the [[Jabbar Baghtcheban|Baghcheban]] phonetic hand alphabet, which is a form of [[cued speech]].

== Deaf community in Iran ==
The estimate of the population of the deaf community in Iran varies between 1.5 and 3 million; Siyavoshi (2017) published that the Iranian Department of Health and Welfare reported 200,000 people self-identifying as deaf when registering for social and medical services.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Siyavoshi |first=Sara |date=2017 |title=The Role of the Nondominant Hand in ZEI Discourse Structure |journal=Sign Language Studies |volume=18 |issue=1 |pages=58–72 |jstor=26478212 |issn=0302-1475}}</ref> However, no estimate is available for the number of ISL users in the country.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Choubsaz |first1=Yassaman |last2=Crasborn |first2=Onno |last3=Siyavoshi |first3=Sara |last4=Soleimanbeigi |first4=Farzaneh |date=June 2022 |title=Documenting the Use of Iranian Sign Language (ZEI) in Kermanshah |journal=Proceedings of the LREC2022 10th Workshop on the Representation and Processing of Sign Languages |pages=37–41 |url=https://aclanthology.org/2022.signlang-1.6 |access-date=2024-05-26 |archive-date=2024-05-12 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240512154139/https://aclanthology.org/2022.signlang-1.6/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

== Regional variation ==
ISL is not standardized across the country. For example, the dialect used in [[Kermanshah province]] is largely comprehensible to ISL users in Tehran, but has some minor vocabulary and fingerspelling differences. Researchers have also noted the dialect uses different mouth shapes, which may have arisen from contact with Kurdish speakers.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Choubsaz |first=Yassaman |title=Western ZEI: Iranian Sign Language in Kermanshah |url=https://www.elararchive.org/dk0598/ |access-date=2025-10-26 |website=Endangered Languages Archive}}</ref>

== Recognition ==
According to the [[Center for Human Rights in Iran]], although Iran ratified the [[Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities]] (CRPD) in 2008, the Iranian government had not officially recognized sign language or introduced sign language-related legislation as of 2018.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Amir |date=2018-09-25 |title=Iran Should Fulfill Its UN Commitments and Recognize Sign Language |url=https://iranhumanrights.org/2018/09/iran-should-fulfill-its-un-commitments-and-recognize-sign-language/ |access-date=2025-10-26 |website=Center for Human Rights in Iran}}</ref>

In late 2021, [[Sharif University of Technology]] and [[Islamic Azad University]] released the first academic book on ISL.<ref>{{Cite web|date=2022-01-05|title=The First Iranian Sign Language book Unveiling Ceremony|url=https://fib.iau.ir/en/news/91/the-first-iranian-sign-language-book-unveiling-ceremony|website=Fereshtegaan International Branch Islamic Axad University}}</ref>

== Names ==
In 1980, the dictionary "Culture: Farsi Sign Language For Deaf, 1st Volume" was published by the Iranian National Organization for the Welfare of the Deaf, referring to the sign language used by deaf and hard-of-hearing communities in Iran. In 1984, a university group based in [[Tehran]] published the first of four editions of "Dictionary of Farsi Sign Language: Standardized Signs", although the English cover used the title "Persian Sign Language Collection for the Deaf", and used the terms Farsi Language and Persian Sign Language interchangeably. In 1999, the phrase Iranian Sign Language was first used in a Master's thesis.<ref>{{cite journal |language=fa |first1=Yahya |last1=Madrasi |first2=Maryam |last2=Bijari |year=2011 |script-title=fa:زبان و فرهنگ ناشنوایان تهرانی |trans-title=Language and culture of Tehrani deaf people |script-journal=fa:نامه انسان شناسی |volume=1 |issue=2 |pages=15–46 |id=[[Scientific Information Database|SID]]: [https://sid.ir/paper/66388/fa 66388] |url=http://ensani.ir/fa/article/131467/%D8%B2%D8%A8%D8%A7%D9%86-%D9%88-%D9%81%D8%B1%D9%87%D9%86%DA%AF-%D9%86%D8%A7%D8%B4%D9%86%D9%88%D8%A7%DB%8C%D8%A7%D9%86-%D8%AA%D9%87%D8%B1%D8%A7%D9%86%DB%8C |access-date=2022-12-19 |archive-date=2022-12-19 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221219155439/http://ensani.ir/fa/article/131467/%D8%B2%D8%A8%D8%A7%D9%86-%D9%88-%D9%81%D8%B1%D9%87%D9%86%DA%AF-%D9%86%D8%A7%D8%B4%D9%86%D9%88%D8%A7%DB%8C%D8%A7%D9%86-%D8%AA%D9%87%D8%B1%D8%A7%D9%86%DB%8C |url-status=live }}</ref> However, the thesis was written by a hearing author without involvement from the deaf community in Iran.

In 2014, deaf linguist Dr. Ardavan Guity, Abbas Behmanesh, and Jodie Novak created a video describing the linguistic properties of Zaban Eshareh Irani, the transliteration of the Persian phrase meaning Iranian Sign Language. Following the video's release, the term Zaban Eshareh Irani gained traction in social media use, particularly among deaf communities in ethnic groups, such as [[Gilaks]], [[Kurds]], and [[Baloch people]] whose primary language is not Farsi and felt alienated from terms such as Farsi Sign Language.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Guity |first=Ardavan |date=April 2022 |title=Esharani Grammatical Sketch: An Initial Description of the Lexicon and Grammar |journal=Sign Language & Linguistics |volume=26 |issue=2 |pages=332–343|publisher=Gallaudet University |doi=10.1075/sll.00077.gui}}</ref> However ZEI was also problematic, as Persian does not have capitalization or acronyms.

In 2021, Guity and Dr. Sara Siyavoshi, a hearing linguist from Iran, proposed the term Esharani as a new name for the sign language used in Iran, derived from the Persian morpheme ''eshar'' (sign), ''ran'' (Iran), and the suffix -''i'', commonly used for language names in Persian.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Guity |first=Ardavan |date=2021-02-11 |title=Reflections on the names of the sign language of Iran, and a proposal |url=https://acadeafic.org/2021/02/11/sign-language-of-iran/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221219155439/https://acadeafic.org/2021/02/11/sign-language-of-iran/ |archive-date=2022-12-19 |access-date=2022-12-19 |website=Acadeafic |language=en}}</ref>  The sign for Esharani itself is derived from the combination of the signs for "Iran" and "sign", where the non-dominant hand is in the five handshape and the dominant hand moves in a spiral motion with the thumb out over the palm of the non-dominant hand. However the acceptability of the name is still under discussion among the deaf communities in Iran.

== Grammar ==
In Tehrani ISL, sentence order is generally subject-object-verb (SOV).<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last1=Leila |first1=Fayazi |last2=Shahla |first2=Raghibdoust |date=2022-09-23 |title=Negation in Iranian Sign Language (Tehrani Variety) |url=https://jrl.ui.ac.ir/article_27418.html?lang=en |journal=Journal of Researches in Linguistics |language=en |volume=14 |issue=2 |doi=10.22108/jrl.2023.136703.1719 |issn=2322-3413 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250711235523/https://jrl.ui.ac.ir/article_27418.html?lang=en |archive-date=2025-07-11 |access-date=2025-10-26 |url-status=live }}</ref> In the dialect, [[clause]]-level negation is performed using manual gestures at the end of the clause, following the verb, excepting some cases where the verb was used to negate the sentence. Negation could also be performed with a [[Predicate (grammar)|predicate]]; this structure could then be used as an [[affix]] or [[clitic]].<ref name=":0" />

When forming [[relative clause]]s, raised brows are used to indicate a reference point.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Siyavoshi |first=Sara |date=2023-05-10 |title=Raised brows in relative clause constructions in Iranian sign language: A cognitive grammar analysis |url=http://icssjournal.ir/article-1-1564-en.html |journal=Advances in Cognitive Science |language=en |volume=25 |issue=Special Issue |pages=8–0 |doi=10.30514/icss.25.0.5}}</ref> Non-manual markers are also crucial for politeness when forming requests, rejections, and apologies. Among these three categories, squinting is used most frequently for requests, side tilt for rejections, and lip puckering for apologies.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Rahbar |first1=Behzad |last2=Khoshandam Mallati |first2=Masoumeh |date=2024-07-22 |title=Politeness in Iranian Sign Language: Analysis of Non-Manual Features |url=https://jolr.ut.ac.ir/article_98221_en.html |journal=Language Research |language=en |volume=15 |issue=1 |pages=95–121 |doi=10.22059/jolr.2024.365113.666856 |issn=2251-9289}}</ref>
